There is no doubt that accurate information and evidence is critical for building trust within the international development cooperation process. I'm delivering this statement on behalf of Aralis Bellarini from World Vision and of the NGO Committee on Financing for Development. A child-specific ODA tracker can ensure financial flows translate into impactful outcomes for children. Thank you, Chair. I speak on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. The group thanks the co-facilitators for their work on this section of the elements paper, and we take this opportunity to reiterate some of the group's submissions in preparation for the zero draft. We are encouraged by the references in the Elements Paper for enhanced national and international cooperation for SDI development, and would like to reiterate that we would also need effective coordination between technology and other sectors, between public and private actors, and across all levels to steer technological change towards addressing pressing development challenges. FFD4 should encourage the development of digital competencies of public officials and institutions of developing countries and mobilize public and private funds in support of capacity building to address rapid technological change and take actions to prevent brain drain in developing countries. We should ensure an efficient, adequate, balanced, and effective intellectual property framework, which encourages access to STI by developing countries, including through better use of existing and exploring further potential flexibilities. One area not touched on was the need to eliminate unfair practices, such as anti-competitive behaviors, and to foster an open, non-discriminatory, fair, and inclusive environment for scientific and technological development. SDI policies should guide technological development to be labor complementary rather than labor replacing, directing resources to education and training, social protection, and compensatory mechanisms to support workers in their transition. We are pleased to see dedicated recommendations on leveraging FinTech, and we reiterate the need to ensure socioeconomic conditions and build institutional capacities to enable the adoption and development of such financial innovation and technology while ensuring relevant safeguards against anti-competitive behavior, consumer privacy, and financial integrity. We must reduce barriers for developing countries to adopt frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence and recognize the importance of financing to unlock the full potential of digital technologies. FFD4 should also consider the creation of a multilateral fund to stimulate innovation and cooperation, facilitate shared global research, technology transfer, and best practices, such as through joint innovation challenges, and enable developing countries to benefit from new and emerging technologies. Chair, the group will continue to engage constructively in this process, including on the negotiations on the zero draft, which we look forward to. Thank you.

We advocate for international collaboration to map digital gaps, identify investment needs, and ensure development of inclusive national strategies regarding STI. We call for international and regional financing mechanisms to prioritize funding a resilient digital infrastructure, emphasizing gender-sensitive approaches and underserved communities. SDI financing falls short of the recommended 1% of the GDP in many regions. We should develop comprehensive SDI investment plans to attract additional resources and establish clear timelines for achieving universal connectivity. Special emphasis should be given in investing, infusing, and innovating localized climate adaptation technology for the climate vulnerable countries. To prevent further widening digital divide, we emphasize ensuring accessible and affordable technology and collaborative international research and development in the developing countries. We request partners to provide technical assistance to implement large-scale digital literacy programs targeting underserved populations, particularly women and youth. Finally, we call for financing capacity-building support for AI adoption in LDCs and other developing countries, coupled with a regulatory framework to ensure safe and inclusive use of artificial intelligence. I thank you.

Thank you, Chair. Innovations, new technologies, science and research, including data, digital and AI are some of the greatest enablers of SDG progress at our disposal. These enablers can drive the strongest and most cost effective development impact across a broad range of areas. We are supportive of actions in the elements paper to close the digital divide and would therefore like to see digital transformation recognized as a cross-cutting theme for FFD4. Inclusive, responsible, safe, and sustainable digital transformation and AI are critical components of closing the digital divide. And we would like to see this recognized in the outcome document. We must ensure that developing countries are actively involved in the development and regulation of AI. We should build on the actions in the elements paper and emphasize the importance of open access. We support equity, collaboration, and openness in the dissemination of research to ensure that scientists, innovators, and policymakers everywhere can access and contribute to the latest science and evidence. Furthermore, we commit to developing a set of principles to support a more globally effective system for research access, participation, and impact. We support the safe development and deployment of new and existing technologies, tools, and products for the global good, sharing the benefits while managing the risks, and to ensure that products developed are affordable, available, and accessible to those who need it most, including the most vulnerable. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of United Kingdom. Now, I give the floor to the distinguished representative of United States of America, to be followed by Saudi Arabia.

Thank you, Chair. The United States reaffirms its commitment to promoting economic development through science, technology, innovation, and capacity building, while also safeguarding national security and human rights. From combating climate change to enhancing education and health care and bolstering economic growth, these critical tools and emerging technologies can help us to not only meet but exceed our collective aspirations for a sustainable and inclusive future. We recognize the critical role of international collaboration between national governments, development finance institutions, and private actors to close the digital divide. Effective multilateral collaboration requires respect for institutional governance, authorities, and mandates, and for each partner to focus on its comparative advantage. The outcome document should recognize that development finance institutions, multilateral development banks, and the IMF have their own governance structures, mandates, and decision-making processes that are independent of the UN. We appreciate the recognition of the Global Digital Compact's commitment to develop innovative and blended financing mechanisms that can close the connectivity gap and leverage existing initiatives to mobilize resources to accelerate investment in digital infrastructure. Furthermore, we want to reemphasize that the GDC supports governance, digital cooperation, and actions that are open to the active and meaningful participation of all stakeholders, so everyone has a voice in the development and implementation of our shared digital future. We acknowledge that science, technology, and innovation play a critical role in achieving the sustainable development goals and that unregulated technological advances can have unintended consequences. To reap the benefits of innovation while minimizing societal disruption, we must prioritize innovation-led growth and carefully manage workforce transitions related to technology adoption. Simultaneously, regulatory and legal environments must support science, technology, and innovation, as the misappropriation of technology and trade secrets poses a significant threat to progress. To guard against this risk, it is important that technology transfer be voluntary and not forced, and that the terms of the transfer are mutually agreed upon by all parties involved and therefore not coerced. The United States underscores the importance of inclusive multi-stakeholder networks united by a common commitment towards achieving the 2030 Agenda. Finally, the United States reiterates our firm belief that a concise and focused FFD4 outcome document will prove most beneficial in achieving our shared development objectives. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of United States of America. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Saudi Arabia to be followed by the representative of India.

Thank you very much, Chair, and good morning to you and all colleagues. With regards to the section on science, technology, and innovation, we have a couple of points to raise. On the global regulatory frameworks for AI and FinTech, they represent an important step in addressing emerging technologies. However, such frameworks require flexibility in a way to develop and implement national strategies without being burdened by top-down global frameworks that may have an opposite effect and be restrictive in nature. Second, we recommend to encourage global governance frameworks for AI and FinTech while respecting national innovation ecosystems and sovereignty and promoting capacity building to support an equitable technological development. Finally, Chair, and this section of the elements paper needs to be inclusive, taking into account different national circumstances, the pathways and approaches. And we shall not discriminate against any technological solution or option that may contribute to achieving our sustainable development. And this should be an overarching principle in the FFD process and the elements paper and the future documents that will be released by the chair. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Saudi Arabia. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of India to be followed by the representative of France.

Thank you, Chair. Overcoming the twin challenges of development and green growth depends on the interplay of innovation, intellectual property, and open science, along with their equitable access. In this context, the outcome document of FFD4 should emphasize the following reforms in financing mechanisms for STI, IP, and open sciences to make them more accessible, transparent, inclusive, and aligned with societal needs. Equitable and well-structured financing mechanisms are prerequisites for fueling innovation. We encourage innovation grants and subsidies for high-risk projects with a high potential social impact to support the startups and researchers having limited access to funds. Further, the collaborative financing models combining public funding and private investments are crucial to reduce financial risks, particularly for large projects and emerging technologies in EMDEs. Strengthening international cooperation is essential to encourage inclusive and non-discriminatory digital transformation with focus on sharing best practices, exchanging policies, tailoring training programs and technology transfer from developed to developing countries. Introduction and implementation of intellectual property policies that don't act as barriers are needed to form an enabling IP ecosystem, which is both accommodating protection and disseminating knowledge at the same time. Tiered licensing and IP pools and commons are some areas which need to be promoted. Open science is pivotal in making research freely available to all, helping scientists to learn, collaborate, and innovate faster. Therefore, policy reforms for mandating open access for public research and supporting data sharing platforms are important steps forward for making equitable benefits. Strengthening capacity building and enhancing digital connectivity in developing countries is crucial for harnessing data for development, particularly through investments in digital economy and infrastructure. Democratizing technology and promoting digital inclusion by advancing literacy, vocational skills, and access to digital tools, particularly empowering women and youth, is important step towards bridging the digital divide. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of India. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of France, to be followed by the representative of China.

And regarding innovation next, we believe that innovation can be encouraged through the development of a social and solidarity based economy. In this regard, we recall the General Assembly's adoption in April 2023 of a resolution recognizing the contribution of this to the achievement of the SDGs. And it also plays an important role in identifying solutions for innovative solutions adapted to local contexts. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of France. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of China to be followed by the representative of the European Union.

We should insist on innovative development. Strengthen global collaboration and SDI, build a global innovation network, promote the application of emerging technologies and strengthen innovation and technological cooperation among enterprises so as to rejuvenate the world economy. All countries should join hands to promote connectivity in the digital age, accelerate the global green and low carbon transformation and realize sustainable development for all. We should advance open cooperation, uphold the spirit of open science without borders and barriers, promote the free flow of people and resources in the field of STI around the globe, strengthen talent exchanges and cooperation, and build an open and free international scientific and technological cooperation ecosystem. We firmly oppose actions that restrict or hinder STI cooperation or harm the common interest of the international community. We should insist on equality and inclusiveness. The concept of cooperation based on mutual respect, fairness, and equality and non-discrimination should be adhered to. China adheres to the principle of intelligence for good, fairness and universality, practice multilateralism and focuses on capacity building. and has promoted the adoption by consensus at the 78th UNGA, a resolution entitled Strengthening International Cooperation in Capacity Building in AI, put forward a plan for the universalization of capacity building in AI, and launched the Group of Friends on International Cooperation in Capacity Building in AI together with Zambia. We welcome the active participation of all countries and will promote broad partnership and will promote the AI for sustainable development for all countries, I think.

Thank you, Chair. The EU supports efforts to achieve universal and meaningful digital connectivity targets for 2030 and enhanced international collaboration for the full implementation of the global digital compact, including closing the digital divide and promoting secure connectivity. Using public funds as catalysts through innovative financing approaches such as blended finance and guarantees will help maximize digital investments. We should like to see greater focus on the role of MDBs and DFIs and agencies in supporting science and technology and innovation. We welcome the reference in the Elements Paper on facilitating access to finance for fintech. Also startups, innovative SMEs, and research infrastructure should be included in this effort. Thank you, Chair. The means of implementation of the 2030 agenda are no less important than financing for development. Thank you, Chair. Germany welcomes the elements paper as a valuable contribution to ongoing discussions on new scientific developments and technological innovations such as artificial intelligence. Innovation, technological and scientific developments have the potential to act as catalysts for development across all sectors and SDGs. However, we need to collaborate to ensure these developments help close digital divides between and within countries rather than widening them. Voluntary technology transfer can contribute to sustainable development when conducted on mutually agreed terms and while ensuring intellectual property rights. Accessible and inclusive capacity building can drive innovation for the social ecological transformation. However, governments and their development partners need to prioritize gender inclusive approaches and this should also be reflected in the zero draft. Since the adoption of the Addis Ababa Action Agenda, there has been significant technological development. AI is such a key development with the potential to empower local ecosystems in sectors like agriculture, education, and efficient resource use. We can only leverage AI's full potential if we ensure equitable access and adhere to responsible and sustainable AI principles. We must take care not to reinforce systemic inequalities, for instance, due to algorithmic biases towards vulnerable groups. We see this balanced approach to AI well reflected in the Elements paper. Digital public goods and digital public infrastructure are key drivers of inclusive transformation and innovation. We support the development of open source software and open data sets in key areas for achieving the SDGs. Germany also welcomes the Global Digital Compact and urges to ensure alignment of language with its paragraph 16 and 17E referencing the need to increase investment and funding for digital public goods and infrastructure. Germany welcomes the elements paper suggestion to realize the full potential of financial technologies in achieving financial inclusion and financial health. Thank you, Chair. Good morning, distinguished delegates. Indonesia is pleased to engage in this important discussion. In this spirit, we wish to share a few constructive comments regarding the paper. First, we must strengthen our regulatory frameworks and environments while ensuring proper governance. Indonesia has developed several regulations related to fintech. licensing, consumer protection, and payment systems. As a result, the number of fintech companies in Indonesia grew significantly from 51 active players in 2011 to 334 in 2022. Additionally, fintech transactions show remarkable growth with over 7.3 billion US dollar processed through electronic money and 3.5 billion US dollar via quick response code in Indonesia. standard. We believe this effort will promote collaboration between local banks and fintech firms as well as draw investment into underserved markets. Second, scaling up investment in both physical and non-physical digital infrastructure is crucial. While this may require significant resources, we believe they will have a lasting impact on achieving the SDGs. For instance, we completed the Palapa Ring project in 2019 to connect more than 500 with 4G internet access. As a result, we saw over 41 million users and 29 million merchants have actively participated in our financial technology services, many of whom are MSMEs enterprises. Besides that, we also conduct national initiatives such as Indonesia FinTech Summit and Expo to promote dialogue between FinTech players and regulators and showcase innovations. We believe these efforts not only reduce the digital divide but also unlock the untapped potential of fintech. Third, we strongly support increasing digital literacy capacity, particularly through initiatives like online universities for developing countries to promote SEEM education. However, we must highlight that this knowledge sharing and capacity building effort is not a one-size-fits-all, so it should be context specific. We need targeted investment to understand local needs with the collaboration of government, civil society, NGOs, and the private sector. In conclusion, Indonesia support the current draft and we are confident our discussion today will lead to tangible outcomes for inclusive science, technology, innovation, and capacity building. I thank you.

Mr. Chair, ladies and gentlemen. The digital divide is a major challenge. Without equitable access to digital technologies in society, many individuals and communities will be left behind. Low and middle income countries are increasingly using digital solution to accelerate progress towards the sustainable development goals. from using data analytics to optimize resource allocation for poverty reduction to e-governance to increase transparency and reduce corruption. Capacity building is crucial to ensure that people have the skills to harness the power of digital tools, which is a key component of Belgium's approach to digital for development, further motivated by a strong focus on this issue in the UN Global Digital Compact. Belgium is committed to a people-centered approach to digital development. This means ensuring that digital technologies are used to empower individuals and communities, reduce inequalities, promote human rights and gender equality, and sustainable development in general. I thank the distinguished representative of Russian Federation. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of European Union, to be followed by the distinguished representative of Islamic Republic of Iran.

Mr President, the EU is committed to free, fair and sustainable trade and to the international rule based system with the WTO at its core. Trade can be a powerful driver of sustainable development and we support strong actions in that vein, with a focus on fostering a level global playing field and resilient, sustainable and inclusive value chains, the benefits of which are widely shared. The EU provides many forms of support to developing countries active participation in the multilateral system, including participation in negotiation in the WTO, as well as effective implementation of agreements such as the Trade Facilitation Agreement. More generally, the EU and its Member States are the world's largest provider of aid for trade, a key tool for sustainable development in line with our global gateway strategy. We provide support for trading capacity of developing countries, for investments in digital and physical infrastructure and for sustainable productive capacity and to improving enabling environment at national, regional and international level. We also provide extensive preferential market access via the GSP, the EPAs and the bilateral trade agreements, and completely duty free, quota free access to LDCs through the EBA. The EU fully supports special and differential treatment for developing countries, in particular LDCs. To make sure that SDT translates to a more level playing field, it should be precise, effective and operational. The WTO agreements recognise two categories of members developing countries and least developing countries. We are in favour of looking into the specific challenges of individual WTO members, but we do not support proliferation of subcategories of developing countries in trade agreements. We absolutely do not agree with one-sided narratives on unilateral environmental trade measures which are designed to support achieving global commitments on climate change. In this respect, the EU's environmental measures are based on thorough impact assessments and carefully designed not to discriminate or treat imports differently from domestically produced products. The EU furthermore engages with its partners actively on these measures, both in the WTO and bilaterally. Openness, transparency and constructive dialogue are key to ensuring the effectiveness of such measures. and also help target support to partners in view of adjusting to them. Thank you very much.

Chairperson, allow me to quote from the outcome of the Africa regional consultation on FFD4 held a few weeks ago. There is a rise in unilateral trade measures, including the CBAM, which discriminate against developing countries by unilaterally imposing sustainability standards on their exports, which threaten not only their exports but production processes within their economies. Africa calls for strengthened multilateral dialogue and cooperation to address climate and trade issues in ways that support rather than hinder developing countries' industrialization efforts. Such measures should be stopped. The strength of the FfD process is that it addresses both the financial and enabling environment dimension, in particular obstacles to development. One such obstacle, which will erase decades of progress and exacerbate poverty, is unilateral environmental trade measures. This is the elephant in the room that FfD 4 needs to address squarely if it is to make a difference to the lives of the poor. We are concerned that the language in section 1E, rather than contributing to solving the problem, instead legitimizes these illegal measures. Impact assessments, as well as due diligence with multilaterally agreed rules, should have been done before the horse had bolted. Furthermore, we cannot support the idea of scaling up support to assist countries with compliance, as this amounts to condoning what are illegal measures. We instead call for suspension of the implementation of CBAMs, as was done with the deforestation regulation, to allow for a cooperative multilateral solution. FFD4 should specifically call for mandated bodies to be set up at the UNFCCC on trade and climate change and for the WTO working group on trade and climate to be strengthened. CBAMs, however, present developing countries with an opportunity to reflect on whether the new economy, or so called green transition, ought to operate in the same way as the fossil fuel and raw material industries have to date. Should strategic minerals and rare earths simply be handed over at low cost to developed countries, or should they be sold at real value or be utilised for local industrialisation and the creation of local value chains, as contained in the UNSG's position paper on resourcing the energy transition towards equity and justice. In this regard, we warmly welcome the section on trade in critical minerals and commodities in the elements paper, including support for the recommendations of the SG's panel on CETMs, which will contribute to ensuring that FFD results in a meaningful outcome by igniting a new growth path for developing countries. Thank you.

Distinguished Madam Chair, delegates, now the international trade is facing unprecedented challenges. In recent years, tariffs on international trade have become increasingly frequent worldwide. This policy, guided by unilateralism and protectionism, not only disrupts the normal operation of international trade rules, but also weakens the possibility of financing development through trade. International trade is the engine of global economic growth and prosperity, an important bridge for promoting connectivity among countries, and a crucial means of promoting development and supporting developing countries. The increase of tariffs and other trade barriers has not only restricted the free flow of goods and services, but also posed a threat to the stability of the global industrial chain and supply chain, and ultimately harm the well-being of people in all countries, especially the interests of developing countries and least developed countries. Therefore, as members of civil society, we have the following three suggestions. Firstly, uphold the rule-based multilateral trading system and respect the core position of the WTO as the maker of international trade rules. Establish a transparent, rule-based and non-discriminatory trading system to provide a fair competitive environment for developing countries. We believe that through a fair, just and open trading system, we can achieve more inclusive and sustainable economic development. Secondly, strengthen the punishment for violations of international trade rules. The UN and other relevant organizations, as well as the international community, should publicly and transparently condemn acts that violate international trade rules and call on relevant countries to immediately stop such practices and UN member states to designate punitive measures. This is not only a necessary means to maintain global economic stability, but also a firm defense of global fairness and justice. Thirdly, leverage technological support and the role of the private sector to reduce trade barriers and promote international trade. Strengthen cooperation between international organizations, governments, and the private sector, enhance technical support and capacity building to help developing countries better integrate into the global trading system. Distinguished guests, the process of globalization is irreversible, but its path requires our joint guidance. Trade barriers and protectionism cannot make the world a better place. Only openness and cooperation can bring true prosperity and peace to human society. The employment.
